units.title: Unit 07 — Everyday verbs 1
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 18–19 (PDF pages 22–23).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Grammatical aspects of collocations · everyday verbs make and do
learningObjectives: Choose make with decisions, arrangements, efforts, changes, contributions and similar outcomes.
Choose do with tasks, work, chores, helping actions and their natural noun partners.
Recognise frequent make/do learner errors and use correct prepositions or articles with the whole expression.
Apply verb–noun collocations in original situations involving work, study and personal life.

items.pt: organizar os preparativos para uma viagem
items.example: We need to make arrangements for a trip to the research centre.
items.note: Use make arrangements for with plans, travel or practical needs; do arrangements is incorrect.

items.example: We should make a change to the timetable before publishing it.
items.note: Make a change to something; the plural make changes is equally common when several things are altered.

items.example: You must make a choice before the registration closes.
items.note: Make a choice, not do a choice; choose is the equivalent verb.

items.example: Could I make a comment about the latest test results?
items.note: Make a comment about or on something; make comments is the plural form.

items.word: make a contribution to a discussion
items.pt: contribuir para uma discussão; dar uma contribuição ao debate
items.example: Everyone can make a contribution to a discussion, even with a brief question.
items.note: Make a contribution to takes the preposition to; contribute to is a useful verbal alternative.

items.example: The team will make a decision after comparing the designs.
items.note: Make a decision, not do a decision; the related verb is decide.

items.example: I will make an effort to speak more clearly during meetings.
items.note: Make an effort to do something; do an effort is not standard English.

items.pt: inventar uma desculpa; dar uma desculpa
items.example: He tried to make an excuse for missing the deadline.
items.note: Make an excuse often means invent a reason; make excuses can imply repeated attempts to avoid responsibility.

items.example: Joining the running club helped me make friends in the city.
items.note: Use make friends rather than get friends when referring to forming friendships.

items.example: The developers hope to make an improvement to the control interface.
items.note: Make an improvement to something; make improvements is common when several aspects are changed.

items.example: I made a mistake when I entered the motor parameters.
items.note: Make a mistake, not do a mistake; the plural is make mistakes.

items.example: I need to make a phone call before the interview.
items.note: Make a phone call describes placing a call; receive a call describes getting one.

items.example: We are beginning to make progress with the new prototype.
items.note: Progress is normally uncountable in this sense: make progress, not make a progress.

items.pt: fazer o seu melhor; dar o máximo de si
items.example: Just do your best during the technical interview.
items.note: Do your best means make the greatest effort you can; not make your best in this sense.

items.example: Moisture can do damage to sensitive electronic components.
items.note: Do damage to something is a standard verb–noun pairing; the noun damage is usually uncountable here.

items.example: We will do an experiment to measure the motor response.
items.note: Do an experiment is common; carry out or conduct an experiment sounds more formal.

items.pt: fazer exercícios; realizar atividades de prática
items.example: I do exercises to practise new English expressions every evening.
items.note: Use do exercises for learning activities or physical exercises, depending on context.

items.pt: me prestar um favor; me ajudar
items.example: Could you do me a good turn and collect the parcel?
items.note: Do somebody a good turn means help that person in a practical way; the pronoun changes with the recipient.

items.example: Could you do me a favour and check this document?
items.note: Do somebody a favour, not make a favour; favour is British spelling of American favor.

items.example: Incorrect wiring could do harm to the equipment.
items.note: Do harm to expresses a negative effect; do more harm than good means cause more problems than benefits.

items.pt: arrumar o cabelo; fazer o penteado
items.example: She likes to do her hair before leaving for work.
items.note: Do your hair means style or arrange it, not simply wash it; the possessive changes with the person.

items.pt: fazer a lição de casa; fazer as tarefas de casa
items.example: The children do their homework before dinner.
items.note: Do homework is conventional; make homework is incorrect when referring to completing assignments.

items.example: I usually do the ironing while listening to a podcast.
items.note: Do the ironing means iron clothes; use do rather than make for this household task.

items.example: We can do the shopping on Saturday morning.
items.note: Do the shopping means buy routine supplies, often groceries; go shopping emphasises the activity of visiting shops.

items.pt: lavar roupa; cuidar da lavagem das roupas
items.example: I will do the washing after I get home.
items.note: In British English do the washing typically refers to laundry; do the washing-up means wash dishes.

items.pt: fazer um pouco de trabalho; trabalhar um pouco
items.example: I need to do some work on the software before lunch.
items.note: Work is normally uncountable in this sense; say do some work, not make some work.

items.example: My sister does the cooking when we have guests.
items.note: Do the cooking refers to responsibility for preparing meals, like do the washing and do the ironing.

items.example: Try not to make negative comments about a colleague's appearance.
items.note: Make comments about something; negative describes the comments, not a different verb pattern.

units.title: Unit 08 — Everyday verbs 2
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 20–21 (PDF pages 24–25).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Grammatical aspects of collocations · change-of-state verbs
learningObjectives: Use go with changes in hair, appearance, senses, emotions and light instead of overusing get.
Use turn for colour changes and distinguish go red from turn red in context.
Choose become or get for changes of state, respecting formal register and the partners that prefer become.
Use fall and grow for natural sudden or gradual changes, and correct common get-based learner errors.

items.example: Some people begin to go bald in their twenties.
items.note: Go bald is a common change-of-state expression; get bald is not the usual collocation.

items.pt: ficar grisalho; ficar com cabelos brancos
items.example: My uncle started to go grey when he was thirty.
items.note: Go grey describes hair losing its original colour; British grey is American gray.

items.example: I would go mad if I had to listen to that alarm all day.
items.note: Go mad can be literal but is often informal exaggeration for extreme frustration; get mad may mean become angry, especially in US English.

items.example: The character gradually goes blind in the novel.
items.note: Go blind means lose the ability to see; become blind is another grammatical possibility.

items.example: Without treatment, the character may go deaf in one ear.
items.note: Go deaf describes a change in hearing ability rather than a temporary failure to hear a sound.

items.example: I always go red when someone praises me in public.
items.note: People or their faces go red from embarrassment, heat or emotion; get red is less idiomatic in this use.

items.example: His face went white when he heard the unexpected news.
items.note: Go white is often used of a face becoming pale from fear, shock or illness.

items.example: The sky can go dark very quickly before a storm.
items.note: Go dark can describe a sudden change in the sky or surroundings; it can also be figurative in other contexts.

items.example: The pages of the old manual began to go yellow.
items.note: Paper can go yellow gradually with age; turn yellow is also common.

items.example: The neighbours would go crazy if we played music that loudly.
items.note: Go crazy can express strong excitement or annoyance and is often informal or figurative.

items.example: The white curtains have gone brown from years of dust and smoke.
items.note: Go brown describes a change in colour; the unit's practice includes objects darkening over time.

items.example: The distant hills turn gold in the evening light.
items.note: Turn is natural for changes of colour, particularly in descriptions of light and nature.

items.pt: ficar vermelho; amadurecer e ficar vermelho
items.example: The tomatoes turn red when they are ripe.
items.note: Turn red is common for fruit and other colour changes; go red is especially natural for a person's face.

items.example: Her hair slowly began to turn white as she grew older.
items.note: Turn white is a natural way to describe hair losing its colour or another visible colour change.

items.example: The afternoon sky turned grey before the rain.
items.note: Turn grey describes a colour shift; go dark may emphasise an approaching storm or loss of light.

items.example: She became pregnant shortly after moving to her new home.
items.note: Become pregnant is neutral and suits formal writing; get pregnant is also used, especially informally.

items.pt: envolver-se em um projeto; passar a participar de um projeto
items.example: She hopes to become involved in a project on renewable energy.
items.note: Become involved in takes in; get involved in is a more conversational alternative.

items.pt: envolver-se em um projeto; participar de um projeto
items.example: I want to get involved in a project that helps local schools.
items.note: Get involved in means start participating; become involved in is often more suitable for formal writing.

items.example: He became angry when he realised the data had been deleted.
items.note: Become angry is relatively formal; get angry conveys the same change more conversationally.

items.example: I try not to get angry when something goes wrong.
items.note: Get angry is a natural conversational change-of-state expression; become angry is often more formal.

items.example: Visitors may become bored if the presentation is too long.
items.note: Become bored describes entering a state; get bored is a frequent informal alternative.

items.example: The students get excited whenever they visit the laboratory.
items.note: Get excited is conversational; become excited is possible in more formal descriptions.

items.example: The fictional character became depressed after losing his job.
items.note: Become depressed describes a change in emotional state; do not use fall depressed.

items.example: She became upset when the meeting was cancelled without warning.
items.note: Become upset is fairly formal; get upset is more common in everyday conversation.

items.example: Customers may become impatient during a long delay.
items.note: Become impatient describes a growing state of impatience; get impatient is also natural.

items.example: In the film, the argument becomes violent after several minutes.
items.note: Become violent describes a change in behaviour or a situation; get violent is also used informally.

items.example: Several species could become extinct if their habitat disappears.
items.note: Become extinct is standard; get extinct is incorrect.

items.example: The podcast became popular among young engineers.
items.note: Become popular is natural in both speaking and writing; get popular is not the preferred phrase in careful writing.

items.example: The policy became unpopular after its costs were published.
items.note: Become unpopular expresses loss of public approval; the negative prefix changes the adjective, not the verb.

items.pt: ficar sem moradia; passar a viver sem teto
items.example: Many residents became homeless after the severe floods.
items.note: Become homeless is the normal change-of-state expression; got homeless is not idiomatic here.

items.example: The scientist became famous for her work on batteries.
items.note: Become famous is standard; get famous is informal and less suitable in formal prose.

items.example: He fell ill during the trip and had to return early.
items.note: Fall ill is a conventional expression for becoming ill, often suddenly; get ill is also possible.

items.example: The audience fell silent when the speaker entered the room.
items.note: Fall silent means suddenly stop making noise or speaking; become silent is a more neutral alternative.

items.example: We often change our priorities as we grow older.
items.note: Grow older describes gradual ageing; get older is also widely used.

items.pt: ficar mais alto; aumentar de volume
items.example: The engine noise began to grow louder as the car approached.
items.note: Grow louder describes a gradual increase in sound level; get louder is another natural choice.

items.example: She made new friends during her first month at university.
items.note: Use make friends or make new friends, not get new friends, when forming friendships.

items.pt: ter um infarto; sofrer um ataque cardíaco
items.example: He was worried that his father might have a heart attack.
items.note: Have a heart attack means experience one; get a heart attack is a common learner error.

items.pt: sofrer um infarto; sofrer um ataque cardíaco
items.example: In the novel, the main character suffers a heart attack at work.
items.note: Suffer a heart attack is a more formal alternative to have a heart attack, common in reports.

items.pt: ter um filho; ter uma criança
items.example: They hope to have a child after they finish their studies.
items.note: Have a child means become a parent or have a child in one's family; get a child is not idiomatic here.

items.pt: ter um bebê; dar à luz um bebê
items.example: Her sister is going to have a baby in December.
items.note: Have a baby can refer to giving birth or expecting a baby, depending on tense and context; not get a baby.
